de24_reid.topic: Re-identification of 'anonymous' data: studies and documented cases

claims.text: Sweeney (2000) estimated 87% (216m of 248m) of the US population likely unique on 5-digit ZIP, gender and date of birth, using 1990 Census data; county+gender+DOB 18%; she bought the Cambridge, Mass. voter list for $20
Golle recomputed on 2000 Census: 63% uniquely identified by gender, ZIP, full DOB; 'generally agree' with Sweeney but fewer
Sweeney in 1997 identified Massachusetts Governor Bill Weld's medical records using publicly accessible records
de Montjoye et al. 2013: 15 months of mobility data for 1.5 million people; four spatio-temporal points uniquely identify 95%; uniqueness decays only as ~1/10 power of resolution
de Montjoye et al. 2015 (Science): 3 months of credit-card records for 1.1 million people; four spatiotemporal points reidentify 90%; price raises risk 22% on average; women more reidentifiable
Rocher, Hendrickx, de Montjoye 2019: 99.98% of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset using 15 demographic attributes

Narayanan and Shmatikov: Netflix Prize data on ~500,000 subscribers; with 8 ratings (2 may be wrong) and dates within 14 days, 99% of records uniquely identified; 2 ratings with dates within 3 days suffice for 68%; IMDb cross-match revealed apparent political preferences

NYT Dec 2018: at least 75 companies receive anonymous, precise location data from apps; several claim up to 200 million US devices; locations as often as every two seconds; teacher Lisa Magrin identified; industry says data tied to unique ID not name

NYT Opinion 19 Dec 2019: one file of more than 50 billion pings from 12 million+ phones, 2016-17, Washington/NY/SF/LA; traced a senior DoD official and others; 'child's play to connect real names to the dots'; Paul Ohm: precise longitudinal geolocation 'absolutely impossible to anonymize'

The Pillar bought 'commercially available' location data from an unnamed vendor (2018-2020) and matched it to Msgr Jeffrey Burrill's phone and Grindr use; he resigned July 2021; Grindr called it a 'witch hunt' and said it did not believe it was the source

FTC Office of Technology (July 2024): 'hashes aren't anonymous'; a hash 'still creates a unique signature that can track a person or device over time'; data is anonymous only when it 'can never be associated back to a person'; cases Nomi 2015, BetterHelp, Premom 2023, InMarket 2024
